query: For refractory high-entropy alloys intended for high-temperature service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their mechanical and thermoelastic behavior? Specify a controlled comparison that would reveal the governing cause, the observations predicted relative to a baseline, the applicable boundary conditions, supporting prior evidence, and an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding approximately 0.1 at.% boron during casting of an equimolar HfMoNbTaTiZr refractory high‐entropy alloy promotes the selective precipitation of hexagonal (Hf,Zr)B2 borides along grain boundaries, which enhances grain-boundary cohesion and alters dislocation interactions, thereby improving ductility, yield strength, and shifting the thermoelastic response at high temperatures.
generation.material_initial_state: An equimolar HfMoNbTaTiZr refractory high‐entropy alloy featuring a BCC solid‐solution matrix with inherent grain‐boundary brittleness.
generation.intervention: Introduce a minor addition of approximately 0.1 at.% boron during the casting process to induce intergranular boride precipitation.
generation.conditions: Conduct high-temperature tensile and creep tests between 673 K and 1273 K under controlled strain rate conditions and in atmospheres that minimize oxidation. Include refined in-situ elastic modulus measurement techniques (e.g., high-temperature XRD or mechanical testing setups) for accurate thermoelastic characterization.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of hexagonal (Hf,Zr)B2 boride precipitates along the grain boundaries.
generation.mechanism: The intergranular boride precipitation increases grain-boundary cohesion and alters local dislocation interactions, thereby mitigating grain boundary brittleness and inducing measurable shifts in both mechanical properties (e.g., improved ductility and yield strength) and thermoelastic behavior (e.g., changes in the elastic modulus) at elevated temperatures.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the baseline alloy without boron, the boron-added alloy is expected to exhibit higher ductility and yield strength along with an observable shift in the elastic modulus during high-temperature testing. Failure to detect these improvements or a lack of correlation between the presence of borides and the elastic modulus shift would falsify the hypothesis.
generation.baseline: An equimolar HfMoNbTaTiZr alloy fabricated without boron, exhibiting typical grain-boundary brittleness and standard thermoelastic behavior of BCC refractory high‐entropy alloys.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is applicable under high-temperature (673–1273 K) testing conditions, with measurements specifically targeted under controlled strain rates and protective atmospheres. The results are bound to the studied alloy system and the defined processing and testing parameters.
generation.uncertainty: There is uncertainty regarding the precise magnitude of the elastic modulus shift induced by boride precipitation and the extent to which this effect can be isolated from other temperature‐dependent phenomena. The proposed refined in-situ measurements should help reduce this uncertainty.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of equimolar HfMoNbTaTiZr alloys: one set with 0.1 at.% boron added and one control set without boron. Perform high-temperature tensile and creep tests between 673 K and 1273 K while using refined in-situ elastic modulus measurements (e.g., high-temperature XRD or mechanical test setups) to record thermoelastic properties. Post-test, perform microstructural analysis (using SEM/TEM) to confirm the precipitation of hexagonal (Hf,Zr)B2 borides along the grain boundaries.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the boron-added alloy does not demonstrate statistically significant improvements in ductility or yield strength compared to the control, or the in-situ measurements fail to reveal a measurable shift in the elastic modulus correlated with boride precipitation, then the hypothesis would be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractTo develop strong refractory high-entropy alloys for use at elevated temperatures as well as to overcome grain-boundary brittleness, an equimolar HfMoNbTaTiZr alloy was prepared, and a minor amount of boron (0.1 at.%) was added into the alloy. The microstructures of the alloys were characterized, and their macro-to-microscale mechanical properties were measured. The microstructural observations indicated that the matrices of both the alloys were composed of a body-centered cubic solid-solution structure, and the added boron induced the precipitation of hexagonal close-packed borides (most likely the (Hf, Zr)B2) at the grain boundaries. The modulus and hardness of differently oriented grains were about equivalent, suggesting a diminished anisotropy, and many small slips occurred on multiple {110} planes. While the hardness of the matrix was not increased, the intergranular precipitation of the borides markedly raised the hardness of the grain boundaries. Owing to the enhanced grain boundary cohesion, the work hardenability and ductility were effectively improved with the addition of boron.Keywords: refractory alloy, high-entropy alloy, boride, grain boundary, mechanical prop

Boron has also been widely added in alloys to improve the cohesive strength of grain boundaries [], e.g., to change the fracture mode of Ni3Al from intergranular to transgranular and thus prevent early failure [], or to lower the migration rate of grain boundaries and inhibit grain growth at high temperatures []. Additionally, the short-range order in an Fe40Mn40Co10Cr10 alloy caused by the addition of boron atoms or the precipitation of borides was reported to retard the motion and increase the density of dislocations [], and the discontinuous intergranular precipitation of borides in high-strength steels avoided the intergranular fracture [], both improving the mechanical properties of the alloys [,]. As the grain-boundary brittleness is a major issue for BCC RHEAs, a minor amount of boron element (0.1 at.%) was hence added into an HfMoNbTaTiZr RHEA in the present study for potential precipitation of borides at the grain boundaries and improvement of grain boundary cohesion, then to yield a larger work hardenability and better ductility.

An equimolar HfMoNbTaTiZr RHEA was developed in this study, and the addition of a minor amount of boron (0.1 at.%, RHEA-B) further overcame the grain-boundary brittleness. As indicated by the microstructural observations and chemical analyses, a simple BCC-phase, solid-solution structure was formed in the matrices of both the alloys. The addition of boron did not obviously increase the hardness of the matrix but induced the intergranular precipitation of the HCP-phase (Hf, Zr)B2 borides which markedly raised the hardness of the grain boundaries. Attributable to the lattice distortions caused by the random distribution of different constituent elements, a diminished anisotropy in the mechanical properties was noticed, and the deformation behavior was mediated by many small slips on multiple {110} planes. Owing to the enhanced grain boundary cohesion with the addition of boron and the intergranular precipitation of borides, the work hardenability and ductility of the alloy were effectively improved, and the failure mode obviously changed from a mainly intergranular facture to a major portion of the transgranular fracture.

proposals.intervention: Introduce a minor addition of boron (≈0.1 at.%) during casting to promote intergranular boride precipitation
proposals.conditions: High-temperature tensile and creep tests (e.g., 673–1273 K) under controlled strain rates and atmospheres to minimize oxidation
proposals.structural_mediator: Formation of hexagonal (Hf,Zr)B2 boride precipitates along grain boundaries
proposals.mechanism: The boride precipitation enhances grain-boundary cohesion and modifies the local dislocation interactions, thereby altering both the mechanical (ductility, yield strength) and thermoelastic properties by mitigating grain-boundary brittleness
proposals.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline unmodified alloy, the boron-added alloy will exhibit higher ductility and improved yield strength at elevated temperatures, with an observable shift in the elastic modulus. If the mechanism is valid, failure to observe improved ductility or altered modulus would falsify the hypothesis
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: This controlled comparison isolates the effect of grain-boundary strengthening (mediated by precipitated borides) on thermoelastic and mechanical behavior, providing a testable mechanism for the performance of RHEAs at high temperatures

proposals.intervention: Conduct systematic molecular dynamics simulations alongside complementary high-temperature tensile experiments varying strain rate and temperature
proposals.conditions: Testing over a range of temperatures (e.g., from cryogenic to 873 K) and strain rates to provoke different deformation modes (grain-boundary slip versus dislocation slip) and trigger phase transformations
proposals.structural_mediator: Temperature-induced structural transition from a body-centered cubic (BCC) matrix to a face-centered cubic (FCC) phase along with associated dislocation reactions
proposals.mechanism: A temperature‐ and strain rate–dependent transition in the active deformation mechanism (from dominant grain-boundary slip at high T/low strain rate to dislocation slip and phase transformation at low T/high strain rate) governs the thermoelastic response and mechanical strength
proposals.predicted_outcome: The alloy is predicted to show a marked change in elastic modulus and yield strength corresponding to the onset of phase transformation. Failure to observe BCC to FCC transformation or a clear shift in deformation mechanism would falsify the hypothesis
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: By directly correlating phase transitions and dislocation behavior with mechanical and thermoelastic measurements, this approach reveals the governing cause for the material performance under different thermal conditions

proposals.intervention: Implement controlled high-strain compression tests and concurrent high-temperature annealing to trigger a clustering-to-ordering transition
proposals.conditions: High-strain deformation under controlled temperatures (using in-situ TEM or post-mortem analyses at several temperatures, e.g., 673 K to 873 K), comparing samples deformed under compression versus tension
proposals.structural_mediator: Atomistic clustering that evolves into a more ordered state under high-strain conditions
proposals.mechanism: High-strain induced atomistic rearrangements lead to a clustering-to-ordering transition that enhances the local bonding environment, thereby modifying the stiffness and thermoelastic constants of the alloy
proposals.predicted_outcome: In the compressed samples, one expects an increased elastic modulus and shifting yield points due to ordering, while tension-loaded samples may not show this transition. Absence of clustering-to-ordering or no measurable impact on the elastic constants would falsify the hypothesis
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: This direct microstructural control experiment links high-temperature mechanical performance with local ordering phenomena, offering a mechanistic explanation for thermoelastic behavior of RHEAs

proposals.intervention: Engineer controlled thermal gradients during processing to induce variable entropy generation and self-organized boundary defect patterns via a MEPR-guided approach
proposals.conditions: Apply in-situ thermal cycling and localized heating during post-processing (annealing between 700 and 1200 K) and then perform high-temperature mechanical tests in inert atmospheres
proposals.structural_mediator: Self-organized boundary defects and discontinuous pattern changes within the microstructure as governed by the maximum entropy production rate principle
proposals.mechanism: Acceleration of entropy generation and export across boundaries induces a sudden reorganization of the microstructure, leading to distinct thermoelastic stiffness and mechanical strength regimes. This self-organized transition should be observable as discontinuities in the stress–strain and elastic modulus-temperature curves
proposals.predicted_outcome: A controlled comparison between samples with intentionally enhanced versus minimized thermal gradients should reveal a discontinuous change in thermoelastic properties corresponding to the self-organized pattern transition. A lack of significant differences would falsify the hypothesis
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: This approach uses the MEPR and boundary defect self-organization mechanism to directly connect thermodynamic driving forces with observable changes in mechanical and thermoelastic responses at high temperatures

critiques.addresses_problem: Yes. The hypothesis directly links the precipitation of borides with improved grain-boundary cohesion and altered dislocation behavior, which are central to mechanical and thermoelastic performance at high temperatures.
critiques.constraints: It respects the explicit constraints by using the specified equimolar HfMoNbTaTiZr alloy and testing under high-temperature tensile/creep conditions with controlled atmospheres.
critiques.physical_soundness: The mechanism is physically sound. Boron-induced intergranular boride precipitation is known to enhance grain boundary strength and modify mechanical responses, as supported by prior studies.
critiques.feasibility: The approach is feasible with established casting, microstructural characterization, and mechanical testing methods.
critiques.evidence: Prior work (e.g., record IDs PMC9572892 from abstract, conclusions, and introduction) directly supports the role of boron in inducing beneficial boride precipitation.
critiques.main_risk: The main risk is that although enhanced grain boundary cohesion is demonstrated, the predicted shift in the elastic modulus (thermoelastic behavior) may be subtle or masked by other temperature‐dependent effects.
critiques.fix: Include a more refined measurement protocol (e.g., in-situ elastic modulus measurements) to unambiguously capture thermoelastic shifts correlated with boride precipitation.

critiques.addresses_problem: Yes. This direction tests the link between a temperature– and strain rate–dependent phase transformation (BCC to FCC) and the corresponding change in mechanical/thermoelastic properties.
critiques.constraints: It meets most constraints with defined alloy composition and testing over a range of temperatures and strain rates, although the highest temperature range may need to align more closely with refractory service conditions.
critiques.physical_soundness: The proposed mechanism is plausible—phase transitions altering deformation mechanisms can significantly change mechanical and thermoelastic responses.
critiques.feasibility: The combined molecular dynamics simulations and high-temperature tensile experiments are established methods; however, detecting a BCC-to-FCC transition in real-world tests may be challenging.
critiques.evidence: Records such as PMC10383748 and PMC6045582 provide support for phase transformation effects on mechanical behavior.
critiques.main_risk: The phase transition may not occur or may be difficult to detect under realistic high-temperature conditions, thereby complicating correlation with thermoelastic property shifts.
critiques.fix: Extend the experimental temperature range or incorporate complementary phase identification techniques (e.g., high-temperature XRD) to reliably verify the BCC-to-FCC transformation.

critiques.addresses_problem: Partially. While it proposes linking entropy generation and self-organized defect patterns to changes in thermoelastic and mechanical properties, the connection to the performance of refractory HEAs is more indirect.
critiques.constraints: The approach fits the specified refractory alloy system and high-temperature conditions but relies on the somewhat speculative MEPR framework.
critiques.physical_soundness: The mechanism is less conventional. The application of the Maximum Entropy Production Rate principle to induce controlled microstructural reorganization in refractory HEAs is innovative but not yet well-established.
critiques.feasibility: Achieving reproducible control over thermal gradients and quantitatively linking defect self-organization to mechanical properties can be challenging with current experimental methods.
critiques.evidence: While the MEPR concept is discussed (e.g., in record PMC8392280), it is not yet firmly established in refractory HEAs.
critiques.main_risk: The primary risk is that the MEPR-guided self-organization may be too subtle or complex to induce clear, falsifiable shifts in thermoelastic and mechanical properties.
critiques.fix: Integrate direct, high-resolution microstructural characterization (e.g., in-situ TEM or synchrotron studies) to validate and quantify the defect patterns associated with the prescribed thermal gradients.

critiques.addresses_problem: Partially. Although it proposes a mechanism (clustering-to-ordering transition) that could affect mechanical and thermoelastic properties, it is based on an alloy (Al0.1CrCoFeNi) that does not meet the refractory high-temperature criterion.
critiques.constraints: This direction violates the explicit constraint regarding the material system since Al0.1CrCoFeNi is not a refractory HEA and is commonly studied for room-temperature applications.
critiques.physical_soundness: Within its own system, the mechanism is physically plausible as supported by simulations and experiments showing clustering-to-ordering transitions under compressive loading.
critiques.feasibility: The high-strain compression tests and related analyses are feasible with established in-situ TEM and mechanical testing techniques.
critiques.evidence: The evidence from records such as PMC4976365 supports the occurrence of clustering-to-ordering transitions under compressive loading in this alloy system.
critiques.main_risk: The main risk is that the mechanism is demonstrated in an alloy that does not qualify as a refractory HEA, hence it may not be applicable to high-temperature service conditions.
critiques.fix: Modify the approach to use a refractory HEA composition that meets high-temperature service criteria, ensuring that the clustering-to-ordering mechanism is investigated in a relevant material system.

decision.rationale: Direction A directly addresses the central question by linking the precipitation of borides to improved grain boundary cohesion and thermoelastic shifts in a refractory high‐entropy alloy. The critic’s review was strongly positive, with a suggested fix to incorporate more refined in-situ elastic modulus measurements to clearly capture the thermoelastic changes. This minor adjustment increases the reliability of the observations without altering the core hypothesis, making A the best candidate.
